scenes.vo: Here's the plan. What a money market actually is, mechanically, and where the yield genuinely comes from. Utilisation, and the kinked interest-rate curve it drives. A full worked example, with a real, verified rate table. And why a sudden spike in rates near full utilisation is a warning sign, not free money.

scenes.title: A pool, not a person on the other side
scenes.sub: Same shape as an AMM, from Module 2.
scenes.vo: The mechanism.

scenes.eyebrow: How a money market actually works
scenes.vo: Here's the mechanism, in full. Lenders supply assets into a shared pool. Borrowers borrow from that same pool, against collateral they've locked up. A smart contract sets the rates on both sides, automatically. And when you supply, you receive a receipt token back, representing your deposit plus the interest it's earning, growing in value the whole time you hold it.

scenes.kicker: Where the yield actually comes from
lines: Not manufactured. A direct transfer, mediated by contract.
scenes.vo: Here's exactly where the yield genuinely comes from, since it isn't magic, and it isn't the protocol's own money. Every dollar a lender earns is a dollar a borrower actually paid, in interest, for the privilege of borrowing against their own collateral instead of selling it. No borrower, no yield. It's a direct transfer, mediated by a smart contract, not manufactured out of nowhere.

scenes.title: What your receipt token actually does

nodes.label: You deposit, receive a receipt token
No separate claim needed
nodes.sub: Interest is baked into the token itself

nodes.label: Redeem for more than you deposited

scenes.vo: Here's exactly what happens to your receipt token, step by step, from the moment you supply. You deposit an asset, and receive a receipt token in return, immediately. That token's exchange rate against the underlying asset climbs continuously, as interest accrues, second by second. You never need to claim interest separately, or take any additional action. And when you eventually redeem it, you receive back more of the underlying asset than you originally put in.

left.label: A traditional bank loan
items: Based on credit history and income

scenes.vo: Worth contrasting this against a traditional bank loan, since it explains why DeFi lending works so differently underneath. A bank lends based on your credit history and income, trusting you to repay over time, with no collateral locked up front. A DeFi money market instead requires collateral worth more than the loan, upfront, and enforces repayment through code, not trust or credit checks.

scenes.q: Where does a lender's yield in a money market actually come from?
scenes.a: Directly from the interest borrowers pay — a transfer, not created money.
scenes.vo: Quick check. Where does a lender's yield in a money market actually come from? [[pause 4]] The answer: directly from the interest borrowers pay to borrow against their collateral. It's a transfer between the two sides, not money created by the protocol.

scenes.title: Gentle, then steep, above one point
scenes.vo: The kinked interest-rate curve.

scenes.title: What utilisation actually drives

nodes.label: Utilisation = borrowed ÷ supplied
nodes.sub: The one number that drives everything here

nodes.label: Below the optimal point
nodes.sub: Rates rise gently, e.g. up to ~80%

nodes.label: Above the optimal point
nodes.sub: The curve kinks: rates rise steeply

nodes.label: Pulls in lenders, pushes out borrowers
nodes.sub: Exactly the point of the kink

scenes.vo: Here's exactly what utilisation is, and what it does, mechanically. Utilisation equals the amount currently borrowed, divided by the total amount supplied. Below a market's chosen optimal point, commonly around eighty percent, rates rise only gently as utilisation climbs. Above that same optimal point, the curve kinks, and rates rise steeply instead, specifically to pull in more lenders and push out some borrowers.

right.label: Above the optimal point
items: Lenders: richer rate, growing liquidity risk
Borrowers: rate that can force unplanned repayment

scenes.vo: Worth naming the trade-off from each side's perspective directly, since “gentle then steep” affects lenders and borrowers differently. A lender below the optimal point earns a modest, steady rate; above it, a much richer one, but with growing liquidity risk attached. A borrower below the optimal point pays a modest, predictable rate; above it, a rate that can climb sharply, fast enough to force an unplanned repayment.

lines: A straight line gives no urgent signal.
The kink makes the pain sharp, exactly where danger begins.
scenes.sub: A design choice, not an accident of the formula.
scenes.vo: Worth being precise about why the curve is deliberately shaped this way, rather than a straight line the whole way. A smooth, straight-line curve gives the market no urgent signal as it approaches full utilisation, the exact moment lenders might not be able to withdraw at all. The kink is a deliberate design choice: make the pain sharp and sudden, specifically where the actual danger, illiquidity, begins.

lines: Supply APY ≈ borrow APY × utilisation × (1 − reserve factor).
The reserve factor is the protocol's own cut.
scenes.sub: Lenders always earn somewhat less than borrowers pay.
scenes.vo: One more piece worth naming before the worked example: supply A.P.Y. is never quite the same as borrow A.P.Y., even at the same utilisation. Supply A.P.Y. is roughly borrow A.P.Y., times utilisation, times one minus the reserve factor, the protocol's own cut. That reserve factor is exactly why lenders always earn somewhat less than what borrowers are actually paying.

scenes.title: Checking a market's kink point yourself
steps: Open the market's own interface or documentation
scenes.result: Not the same on every protocol, or every asset
scenes.vo: Here's how to actually check a market's own kink point yourself, since it isn't the same on every protocol or every asset. Open the market's own interface or documentation directly. Look specifically for its “optimal utilisation” or “kink” parameter, usually shown as a percentage. And compare that number against the market's current utilisation, so you know how much room actually remains before rates start climbing steeply.

scenes.q: Why does the interest-rate curve kink sharply above the optimal utilisation point?
scenes.a: To make borrowing expensive and supplying attractive when liquidity runs low, restoring withdrawal capacity.
scenes.vo: Quick check. Why does the interest-rate curve kink sharply above the optimal utilisation point, instead of rising smoothly the whole way? [[pause 4]] The answer: to make borrowing expensive and supplying attractive right when liquidity runs low, restoring withdrawal capacity before the market actually locks up.

scenes.title: A real, verified rate table
scenes.vo: Worked example.

scenes.title: Borrow APY vs utilisation — the kinked curve
scenes.sub: Illustrative curve: 4% at 80% optimal, +60% slope above

marks.text: The optimal point — the kink itself

scenes.vo: Here's the actual curve, plotted from this specific illustrative example: four percent borrow A.P.Y. at eighty percent optimal utilisation, then a sixty-percent slope above it. At fifty percent utilisation, borrow A.P.Y. is two point five percent. At seventy percent, three point five percent. At eighty percent, exactly four percent, the kink itself. And then it launches: ninety percent utilisation reaches thirty-four percent borrow A.P.Y., and ninety-five percent reaches forty-nine percent.
scenes.cap: Here's the actual curve, plotted from this specific illustrative example: 4% borrow APY at 80% optimal utilisation, then a 60% slope above it. At 50% utilisation, borrow APY is 2.5%. At 70%, 3.5%. At 80%, exactly 4%, the kink itself. And then it launches: 90% utilisation reaches 34% borrow APY, and 95% reaches 49%.

scenes.vo: Now put supply A.P.Y. next to that same borrow A.P.Y., at a ten-percent reserve factor, since lenders never see the full number. At eighty percent utilisation: four percent borrow, two point nine percent supply. At ninety-five percent: forty-nine percent borrow, but supply climbs just as dramatically, to roughly forty-two percent, since supply A.P.Y. scales directly with that same borrow rate.

stats: utilisation events with reported withdrawal delays, on major markets (outside research)
scenes.vo: One real, dated event, so this isn't a hypothetical risk. Major lending markets have genuinely experienced episodes of utilisation pushing well above ninety percent during periods of high demand, with supply rates spiking sharply and withdrawal delays reported by users. This is outside research, not this program's own data, but it's exactly the scenario this worked example is built to help you recognise before it happens to you.

lines: Lenders may not be able to withdraw. A warning, not a gift.
scenes.sub: The money is out. It hasn't disappeared — it just isn't liquid, right now.
scenes.vo: And here's the actual warning hidden inside that second number. A sudden forty-two-percent supply A.P.Y. looks like an incredible yield, right up until you remember what it actually means: the pool is nearly fully borrowed, and lenders may simply not be able to withdraw, because the money is out, lent to borrowers who haven't repaid yet. A sudden high supply APY is often a warning, not a gift.

scenes.title: What actually unfolds, near full utilisation

nodes.label: Lenders try to withdraw
nodes.sub: Drawn by the high rate itself

nodes.label: Available liquidity shrinks
nodes.sub: Most of the pool is already lent out

nodes.label: Withdrawals queue, or fail
nodes.sub: Until borrowers repay, or new supply arrives

scenes.vo: Here's exactly what unfolds, step by step, as utilisation actually climbs toward one hundred percent, so “lenders may not be able to withdraw” isn't just a phrase. Utilisation climbs past the optimal point. Rates spike steeply, exactly as the kink is designed to do. Some lenders, seeing high rates, try to withdraw, but the pool's available liquidity is shrinking. And once utilisation is high enough, some withdrawals simply queue, or fail outright, until borrowers repay or new supply arrives.

scenes.q: Utilisation is 99%. What's the actual risk for lenders?
scenes.a: Withdrawals may be blocked until borrowers repay or new supply arrives.
scenes.vo: Quick check. Utilisation on a lending market is ninety-nine percent. What's the actual risk for lenders right now? [[pause 4]] The answer: withdrawals may be blocked entirely, until borrowers repay or new supply arrives, since almost all of the pool's assets are currently lent out.

scenes.title: Your checklist
steps: Check utilisation before supplying, not after
Know the market's specific optimal-utilisation kink
Treat a sudden rate spike as a warning, not a gift
scenes.vo: Here's your checklist. Do it now, before supplying to any market. Check the market's current utilisation before you supply, not after. Know that specific market's optimal-utilisation kink, since it isn't the same everywhere. And treat any sudden rate spike as a liquidity warning to investigate, never as free money to celebrate.

scenes.title: Recap
items: A money market: lenders supply, borrowers borrow, a contract sets rates
Yield is a transfer from borrowers — not created money
The curve kinks deliberately above the optimal utilisation point
A sudden rate spike near full utilisation: a warning, not a gift
scenes.vo: Let's recap. A money market is a pool: lenders supply, borrowers borrow against collateral, a contract sets both rates. Every dollar of yield a lender earns is a dollar a borrower actually paid; it's a transfer, not created money. The interest-rate curve kinks deliberately above an optimal utilisation point, to protect withdrawal capacity right when it matters most. And a sudden spike in supply APY, near full utilisation, is a liquidity warning first, an opportunity second, if at all.
